headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: agent A’s marketing workspace can feed agent B’s secret-handling RAG workflow, while both can write files and run subprocesses.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can write/read files and its sandboxing says skills “reference each other and build on shared context”; agent B reads files, uses stdin/stdout, and runs a LangGraph subagent model. That creates a plausible file-based instruction bridge. No direct shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests files produced by agent_a without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF a shared workspace is mounted between the two agents, attacker-controlled text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Add a provenance header to every file passed from A to B.
Require B to treat A outputs as untrusted data, not instructions.
Isolate workspaces so A cannot write into B’s input directory.
Review any shared prompt templates for instruction-like file parsing.
requires-engineering: add content filtering or signed artifacts between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles configuration secrets and multiple API keys, while agent A can read/write files and call APIs. If they share a workspace or credentials directory, A can expose B’s secrets or marketing context. Because B’s secret handling is documented and A’s filesystem access is broad, the leakage pathway is credible in default local-development setups.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same project directory, A can read files containing B secrets.
IF B stores API keys in files under its workspace, A can exfiltrate them via filesystem access.
mitigations: Move secrets to an OS keychain or env-only injection.
Separate the agents into distinct directories and volumes.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
Restrict A to a read-only view of non-secret inputs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret mounts and access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, so concurrent edits to shared files are plausible. Agent A also supports multiple instances, and agent B runs in a local development environment with multiple instances supported. No locking is documented, but B does not modify git state, so this is below high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF a shared notebook or config file is edited concurrently, one agent can overwrite the other’s changes.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Use file locks for any shared artifacts.
Serialize writes to notebooks and configs.
Keep generated outputs in per-agent subfolders.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A’s marketing outputs can become inputs to agent B’s RAG or agentic-ask flows, and B exposes endpoints that can act on retrieved content. That makes unverified A output a plausible upstream source for downstream actions. The pair is not documented as directly integrated, so I keep this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as retrieval context or prompt context, errors can cascade.
IF B’s agentic-ask path acts on A’s fabricated facts, downstream outputs can be wrong.
mitigations: Require B to cite source documents before acting on A output.
Add a verification step between A and B.
Flag A-generated content as draft-only.
Limit B to retrieval, not autonomous action, for shared tasks.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking or approval gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles configuration secrets and may process research data, while agent A handles marketing/product-marketing context. The profiles do not show a residency mismatch, but B’s secret and API handling plus local-development deployment create retention and access-control concerns if shared with A. Because the compliance boundary is undocumented, uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF regulated or confidential data is placed into the shared local development environment, retention and access controls may be violated.
IF B’s secrets are logged or copied into A’s workspace, compliance obligations can be breached.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared environment.
Disable verbose logging for secrets and prompts.
Review retention settings for notebooks and API logs.
Separate marketing content from secret-bearing project files.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls per agent.
